3 Singapore REITs Rewarding Unitholders with Higher DPU
article:
Earnings season is when real estate investment trust (REIT) investors find out whether rents kept pace with borrowing costs.
Not every
Singapore REIT
passed that test this time round.
Three did, and raised their distribution per unit (DPU) in the process.
The three REITs report over different periods.
Compare the direction of each trend, not the size of the numbers.
Can Frasers Centrepoint Trust keep raising its payout?
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), or FCT, is Singapore’s largest suburban retail mall owner.
Its eight malls include Northpoint City, Causeway Point and Waterway Point.
For the fiscal year ended 30 September 2026 (FY2026), gross revenue rose 14.2% year on year (YoY) to S$444.9 million.
Net property income (NPI) grew 15.7% to S$321.7 million.
DPU climbed 2.0% YoY to a record S$0.1235.
NPI grew far faster than DPU.
Northpoint City South Wing, which FCT bought in May 2025, contributed for a full year and accounts for most of the NPI increase.
Distributions from joint ventures fell 11.7% YoY because a one-off special dividend did not recur.
The malls themselves are in good shape.
Retail committed occupancy stood at 99.7% as at 30 September 2026.
This excludes the  divested White Sands and NEX, which is undergoing an asset enhancement initiative (AEI).
Rental reversion for FY2026 came in at 6.6%.
FCT is also borrowing more cheaply.
Its average cost of debt fell to 3.2% from 3.8% a year ago.
FCT sold White Sands on 30 September 2026 and will use the proceeds to repay borrowings.
That will cut aggregate leverage from 38.7% to 36.8%.
The thing to watch is the AEI pipeline.
NEX’s first-phase upgrade is 98% pre-committed and due to finish in December 2026.
Causeway Point’s AEI is due to start in the second quarter of 2027.
Upgrades take space offline while work is under way, and that can slow income growth for a while.
The payoff can be worth it.
The completed Hougang Mall AEI delivered a return on investment of about 8%.
Is Keppel DC REIT’s growth worth the extra debt?
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) owns 27
data centres
across 10 countries, with Singapore and Japan being its two largest markets.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), gross revenue rose 13.3% YoY to S$365.3 million.
NPI increased 13.1% to S$316.8 million.
DPU grew 11.7% YoY to S$0.0857.
Positive rental reversions and escalations lifted NPI.
Rental reversion averaged around 14% for 9M2026, and portfolio occupancy improved to 93.0% from 92.5% in 2Q2026.
Tokyo Data Centre 3 added to NPI, while larger stakes in Keppel DC Singapore 3 and 4 meant more of that income flowed to unitholders.
On the flip side, Keppel DC REIT lost income from Kelsterbach Data Centre, sold in March 2025, and from Cardiff Data Centre, where the client’s contract expired in June 2026.
Finance costs rose 28.1% YoY.
There’s a per-unit effect to note too.
A larger unit base after the September 2026 private placement diluted DPU because the new units arrived before the new Tokyo assets started contributing income.
In other words, the 11.7% DPU growth came despite a timing drag that should fade.
That placement funded part of a bigger move.
On 1 October 2026, Keppel DC REIT completed the purchase of an 88.62% effective interest in Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5 for around S$1.4 billion.
Both assets are fully occupied, and their in-place rents sit more than 30% below market.
Management expects the deal to lift DPU by 2.0%.
The trade-off is leverage.
A S$625 million private placement paid for part of the deal, and yen-denominated debt covered the rest.
Aggregate leverage stood at 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 and rose to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.
Those below-market Tokyo rents are the key: they need to reset higher over time to cover the bigger interest bill.
What’s behind Suntec REIT’s higher DPU?
Suntec REIT
(SGX: T82U) owns 10 office, retail and convention properties across Singapore, Australia and the UK.
For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026) ended 30 September 2026, gross revenue rose 5.2% YoY to S$123.6 million.
NPI increased 6.2% to S$83.4 million, while DPU climbed 13.4% YoY to S$0.02017.
Keep in mind that these figures cover a single quarter.
DPU grew more than twice as fast as NPI.
Lower financing costs help explain that gap.
Suntec REIT’s Singapore offices and malls drove the quarter.
Committed occupancy for the Singapore office and retail portfolios stood at 99.6% and 98.6% respectively.
Rental reversions came in at 7.3% and 11.2% respectively.
Tenant sales per square foot at Suntec City Mall rose 10% YoY.
Australia is where things get interesting.
Backfilled leases at 177 Pacific Highway and higher occupancy at 477 Collins Street also added to income this quarter.
Suntec REIT now wants to sell both, along with 21 Harris Street.
It has launched sales campaigns for all three to reduce overseas exposure.
For income investors, that cuts both ways.
Selling these buildings would remove some of the income that helped this quarter.
Its aggregate leverage rose to 43.0% as at 30 September 2026, from 41.5% at end-2025.
Management lists lower leverage and unit buy-backs among its capital management options.
Whether DPU holds up from here will depend on the sale prices and where the money goes.
Get Smart: Find out where the DPU growth comes from
A rising DPU is good news, but where the increase comes from matters more.
Growth from higher rents at existing properties can repeat year after year.
Growth from cheaper debt or a newly bought asset deserves a second look.
Interest rates can rise again, and an
acquisition
only pays off if the REIT didn’t overpay.
All three REITs here raised rents.
FCT and Suntec REIT also borrowed more cheaply.
Keppel DC REIT issued more units and took on more debt to expand in Tokyo.
So the next time a REIT raises its payout, check whether rental reversions are positive and whether leverage is climbing.
When rents are rising and leverage is steady, you’re looking at a distribution with room to grow.

title: Nvidia boosts chip tracking in Southeast Asia to fight smuggling — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 6): Nvidia Corp is stepping up monitoring of artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators sold in Southeast Asia, a strategic step to curtail semiconductor smuggling after criticism it hasn’t done enough to stop shipments from illegally reaching Chinese companies.

The chipmaker now requires customers in the region to enrol in its so-called fleet intelligence system — which tracks the location of AI accelerators owned by participating companies, among other metrics — in order to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners, or NCPs, according to people familiar with the matter.

The NCP designation is highly coveted for AI cloud computing providers, granting both a public stamp of approval and preferred chip access from a company that plays kingmaker to the industry. Nvidia’s idea is to use the carrot of that label to encourage broader uptake of what remains a voluntary chip tracking programme, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss a confidential new measure.

That could provide more visibility into how Nvidia hardware moves through a region that’s long been a transshipment point for restricted goods. The US government broadly prohibits Chinese companies from purchasing advanced Nvidia AI chips without a licence, though authorities believe firms there have nonetheless gotten their hands on billions of dollars’ worth of the hardware, primarily via smuggling networks in Southeast Asia.

As cases mount, Nvidia and some US authorities have sparred over who is responsible for solving the problem. Corners of Washington are frustrated that the chipmaker has repeatedly missed red flags, while Nvidia has shot back that it follows laws as written — putting the onus on government officials to identify bad actors. Those officials, meanwhile, disagree on the appropriate tack for their own response, with frustration brewing in the Trump administration and on Capitol Hill.

There is no better illustration of the quagmire than Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, which has been under US and Singapore investigation for more than a year and returned to the limelight last week after The New York Times reported that Washington suspects one of the company’s top executives of spying for Beijing, leveraging her close relationship with Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

See also: AI elite lose US$18 bil as chip stock rout spreads to Asia

In response, Huang said his interactions with Megaspeed were “completely normal”, while an Nvidia spokesperson said the chipmaker is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know”. That aligns with Nvidia’s posture on earlier chip diversion suspicions; the chipmaker said last year that it asked the US government whether it needed to alter its relationship with Megaspeed, and was told no. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Nvidia’s response hasn’t satisfied Capitol Hill, where key House Republicans this week requested a briefing from the CEO.

The status of Nvidia’s own due diligence on Megaspeed — concerning the smuggling suspicions, rather than espionage — is also unclear. Huang said last week that “we’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one”, referring to graphics processing units. That goes a step beyond previous statements on the matter from Nvidia, which said last year — after getting pressed about discrepancies in Megaspeed’s data centre footprint — that it had identified “substantially” all the products sent to the company.

See also: OpenAI to change how it handles data centres after outcry

Nvidia also pledged in December 2025 to visit Megaspeed’s data centres again in the near future, but since then has repeatedly declined to say whether such checks have occurred. That’s even after Megaspeed’s main computing hub landlord dropped it as a tenant and two other data centre operators in Southeast Asia disputed Nvidia’s account of the location of Megaspeed’s chips. Asked again this week whether Nvidia had conducted any additional checks that would support its CEO’s assertions about counting “every” processor, a spokesperson declined to comment.

In the meantime, however, Nvidia has begun flirting with self-regulation. The biggest such example is fleet intelligence — first debuted nearly a year ago, after the US began prosecuting alleged chip smugglers and Washington’s suspicions about Megaspeed became public. It’s primarily a data centre management tool, collecting a range of information about deployments of Nvidia hardware that’s useful for operators. By also gathering geolocation information for individual parts, though, it doubles as a response to US diversion concerns.

The product underscores both that Nvidia has the tools to geolocate its chips and that it remains cautious about using them. For one, fleet intelligence does not by default require participants to share location data with Nvidia or the US government. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told Bloomberg that should Washington regulators want information from the database, they would communicate directly with users, without elaborating further.

A big question for the latest update, related to NCP designations, is whether Nvidia may ultimately require existing NCPs — such as Megaspeed, which won the label within a week of its 2023 creation — to sign up to maintain their privileged status. Nvidia declined to comment on this question or answer others for this story, including whether the new NCP requirement would be applied in regions beyond Southeast Asia.

Outside of fleet intelligence, Nvidia has taken several other steps to limit Chinese companies’ access to its hardware. In the wake of the biggest chip smuggling indictment in the US, the company earlier this year removed half of the Asian firms it had pre-approved for chip purchases, Bloomberg has reported.

More recently, it began telling buyers not to rent more than half of their Nvidia computing power to Chinese companies — even though Washington generally allows Chinese firms to use accelerators owned by others overseas. “Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can,” an Nvidia spokesperson told The Financial Times, which first reported that move. The spokesperson didn’t explain the reasoning behind the new Nvidia measure.

title: Taiwan imposes short-selling limit after stock market rout
article:
(Nov 6): Taiwan rolled out fresh curbs on short selling to rein in market volatility after a deepening selloff in artificial intelligence-related shares drove the island’s benchmark equity gauge into bear-market territory.

The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) capped the volume of intraday short-sale orders for borrowed securities at 3% of a stock’s average daily trading volume over the preceding 30 days, according to a statement on Friday. That’s reduced from 30% previously.

It will also raise the minimum margin requirement for short-selling activities to 130% from 90%. The measures are effective from Nov 9.

Separately, the National Financial Stabilization Fund will activate measures to stabilise the stock market, the Ministry of Finance said earlier on Friday.

“Continued selling by foreign investors has also pointed to a significant deterioration in market confidence.” Finance Ministry said in its statement. It will deploy funds to support market stability as conditions warrant.

Taiwan’s authorities have previously turned to trading curbs during bouts of severe market turmoil, most recently in 2025, when concerns over Donald Trump’s tariff policies roiled global equities.

See also: Tech millionaires fuel BNP’s expansion in Taiwan wealth hiring

The benchmark Taiex index plunged as much as 9% on Friday, with the deepening losses plunging it into the bear market.

Heavyweight Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co led the slump, dropping in tandem with a broader rout in global semiconductor shares amid mounting concern over a potential slowdown in US data-center capital spending.

Premier Cho Jung-tai told reporters ahead of a legislative session on Friday morning that he had directed the FSC to monitor equity-market developments closely and respond flexibly.

title: ‘Anti-AI’ trade turns Indian equities into Asia’s bright spot
article:
(Nov 6): For months, investors touted Indian equities as a place to hide if the global artificial-intelligence trade unravelled. This week, that thesis has played out.

The NSE Nifty 50 Index jumped 2% on Friday, bucking a selloff that left most major Asian markets in the red. As investors slashed exposure to AI stocks on fears of tighter regulation following a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections, Indian equities headed for their biggest weekly gain in more than five years.

It’s a striking reversal for the US$5.3 trillion market in less than two weeks. India’s relative lack of exposure to the AI trade had helped make its stocks among Asia’s worst performers. Now, as the once-high-flying trade unravels, that weakness has quickly turned into a blessing. Global funds are returning, helping narrow year-to-date losses, while plunging oil prices and an improving earnings outlook lift the market’s appeal.

There’s “very high possibility that India market will outperform other Asia markets in the short term,” said Charlie Hong, founder and chief investment officer at LOGOS Asset Management. “The trend will sustain for the medium term only if earnings continue to recover.”

Overseas investors have plowed a net US$1.9 billion into local shares this week through Wednesday, while provisional data for Thursday showed a net inflow of US$1.6 billion. They’re also slashing their bearish wagers — short positions on index futures on the National Stock Exchange of India fell by more than 100,000 contracts this week.

See also: Asia’s richest banker sees AI correction boosting flows to India

The sudden gush of inflows helped propel Indian equities into the ranks of the world’s best performers this week and strengthened the rupee, which neared a record low last month. The currency climbed 0.6% to 93.9175 per dollar, the strongest since April. The dollar-rupee rate has also broken below its 200-day moving average for the first time since 2025.

“Unless the war in West Asia re-escalates, this Goldilocks situation could continue for the rupee,” said Anindya Banerjee, head of research, commodity and currency derivatives at Kotak Neo. “In that situation, once 94 per dollar breaks, we will see a breakout from a range that has held since April and then a lot of panic dollar-selling could happen from exporters.”

See also: German firms Mahle, Schott said to seek banks for India IPOs

Still, Indian shares remain on track for their first annual losses in 11 years, while the rupee is among Asia’s weaker currencies and foreign outflows are still at a record for the year. Energy costs remain elevated, and earnings growth continues to lag peers in North Asia.

The rally has been accompanied by a rise in volatility. A gauge of implied stock swings on the NSE soared 13%, the most since late September.

For now, the plunge in oil prices and improving earnings could provide another tailwind by boosting the appeal of Indian assets. Profit growth at roughly two-thirds of BSE 100 companies that have reported results was the fastest in at least five quarters and beat estimates, according to Citigroup Inc.

“Interest from foreign clients have gone up recently,” said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia strategist at Societe Generale SA. “India is standing out amid a sea of red.”

title: Fed's Williams says should gather data to judge price risks
article:
(Nov 6): Federal Reserve Bank of New York president John Williams endorsed the US central bank’s statement saying that this is the time to collect information on the risks to prices.

Speaking at an event at the European Central Bank in Frankfurt on Friday, he said that inflation is “absolutely too high”, though other indicators so far aren’t signalling concern.

Monetary policy “does have a critical role in making sure that these relative price shocks don’t translate into broader or more persistent inflation,” Williams said. “Inflation expectations remain well anchored. We’re seeing wage growth be consistent with our 2% goal.”

Fed officials held interest rates steady last month, saying the “accumulation of more information” would allow them to determine the best level for policy. The 10-2 decision to stay put followed a unanimous move to lift their benchmark rate in September by a quarter point to a target range of 3.75-4%.

Several policymakers speaking since the meeting have touted the need for additional rate hikes but advocated for a gradual approach. The public statements followed comments from chairman Kevin Warsh, who pointed to a strong economy and warned about persistent inflation, but continued to abstain from sharing his outlook for rates.

“Our FOMC [Federal Open Market Committee] statement last meeting, I think, captures correctly that this is an appropriate time to accumulate more information to help us determine what the appropriate stance of policy is to make make sure we achieve a timely return to our 2% target,” Williams said.

See also: US voters reset debate on data centres and billionaires

The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose by 3.6% in September from a year earlier, and gauges of underlying inflation excluding food and energy items also rose. Data also showed the US economy expanded at the fastest pace in a year in the quarter ending September.

“A couple of themes are really interesting, both for us and around the world: a very unusual set of relative price shocks affecting our economies, at the same time very strong resilience at least our economy through these shocks,” Williams said.

He spoke just days after US Democrats saw decisive victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections, taking control of Congress in a shift that Fed watchers said could protect the central bank and give officials more room to fight inflation without political interference.

title: Tech millionaires fuel BNP’s expansion in Taiwan wealth hiring
article:
(Nov 6): BNP Paribas SA is expanding its wealth management operations in Taiwan and stepping up relationship manager hires, looking to capture a greater share of the island’s swelling fortunes.

“Taiwan is clearly a top, top priority for us,” said Vincent Lecomte, chief executive officer of the European bank’s global wealth management business, citing the island’s fast-growing riches and economic expansion. The lender employs about 150 staff in the division locally, including about 40 relationship managers.

Lecomte said Taiwan is a growth engine for the firm’s overall expansion in the region. Asia accounted for a “significant” share of the €11.5 billion in global net new assets drawn by the wealth unit during the first nine months of the year, he said.

BNP Paribas has €535 billion in global wealth assets under management, with Asia accounting for about 20%, Lecomte said.

The lender’s build-out mirrors moves by rivals including UBS Group AG, HSBC Holdings plc and Standard Chartered plc in chasing wealth created by the island’s boom.

BNP plans to expand its local roster of relationship managers at a “close to double-digit” pace to support similar business growth in the unit. Along with mainland China, Taiwan ranks among the bank’s fastest-growing Asian wealth markets, fuelling broader momentum across Hong Kong and Singapore.

See also: The China advantage: Speed of execution

In Taiwan, “You have more and more millionaires just because they’re employees of TSMC and the ecosystem.” said Arnaud Tellier, CEO of BNP Wealth Management in Asia.

He said rising share prices have lifted local assets managed at the bank, while the wealth effect is rippling through the island’s broader economy, thanks to highly profitable tech companies.

Taiwan’s wealth managers are grappling with a talent crunch, forcing firms to boost compensation as they struggle to fill positions for experienced bankers. Top-tier candidates are fetching sign-on bonuses and guaranteed annual packages of around NT$10 million, according to recruitment firms.

See also: China's crackdown pushes wealthy to gold, lifting Hong Kong jewellery sales

Tellier said the industry’s strong momentum is creating a banker shortage across Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore. Many people express interest in private banking but still lack the required skills, he said. “It’s a challenge.”

Taiwan posted its fourth straight quarter of double-digit economic growth, with gross domestic product expanding 14.36% in the third quarter, the longest such stretch in nearly 39 years.

title: BofA’s Piron sees won, Taiwan dollar as buys after AI rout
article:
(Nov 6): The South Korean won and Taiwan dollar offer buying opportunities after the artificial intelligence-driven equity selloff, according to Bank of America Corp.

Both currencies have weakened in tandem with AI-linked stocks, but the size of their current-account surpluses gives investors “substantial” cover to build long positions, said Claudio Piron, head of Asia foreign-exchange and rates strategy at BofA’s global research unit.

“That will come into play,” he said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “I would say at the margin that these levels here provide an opportunity for people to enter into long Korean won positions and long Taiwan positions.”

Piron said the Taiwan dollar was the Asian currency most correlated with AI exchange-traded funds, making its recent decline consistent with a positioning squeeze rather than a fundamental deterioration.

On the dollar, Piron said US exceptionalism — the narrative that had driven dollar strength — was linked to AI and had faded for now. He set a dollar-won target of 1,330 for the year-end, and 1,300 for the next quarter.

On stocks, Peter S Kim, KB Financial Group Inc’s global strategist, said South Korea’s equity selloff has created a buying opportunity for investors willing to wait. The chip-heavy Kospi index plunged 6% on Friday, mirroring declines in US tech companies.

See also: Yen regains haven appeal as AI rout sends investors to safety

“I feel very comfortable, for institutional investors, that this is one of those moments that I look at in my career — that risk-reward is now favouring the buyers rather than the sellers,” Kim said in a separate Bloomberg TV interview.

title: Asia hedge funds, rich investors face big losses in AI rout
article:
(Nov 6): Hedge fund managers, brokers and wealthy investors in Asia had a hectic Friday as the sharp selloff in equities reignited fears that the unwinding of artificial intelligence (AI) bets is far from over.

Money managers fielded worried phone calls as losses rippled through some of the market’s most crowded trades. Wealthy clients from Taiwan to Hong Kong faced margin calls on leveraged bets, according to people familiar with the matter. In Hong Kong, some investors braced for steep losses from structured notes as they were forced to take delivery of shares at a loss, they said.

“This is as extreme as almost any I have seen since the dot-com bubble,” said Chris McGuire, who began trading options at the CBOT in 1991. He now manages a Japanese convertible-bond arbitrage fund at Eagle’s View Capital Management. “The unwind by equity holders who all appear concentrated in the same stocks or sectors has created more one-way momentum than we have seen for a long time.”

The wild swings inflicted widespread losses in the hedge fund industry, including for giants such as ExodusPoint Capital Management and Millennium Management, though some benefitted from the volatility. McGuire said his fund gained an estimated 2.5% or more this month.

The larger picture across Asia, however, was downbeat. Hong-Kong based hedge fund Aspex suffered a 16% loss in last month’s technology shares rout, according to people familiar with the matter. In China, long-only quantitative strategies lost more than 10% in October, wiping out their gains for the year, according to a report from China Merchants Futures.

See also: Watch for the double top pattern that precedes a market crash

Goldman Sachs Group Inc prime brokers estimated Asia stock pickers lost 9.4% last month, eroding this year’s gain to 14%. Those focused on China tumbled 11% in October, reducing this year’s return to 16%.

Some other funds saw smaller losses. Valliance Asset Management said in an investor update that its Long-Short Master Fund fell 6.7% in October. CloudAlpha Capital Management’s US$2.8 billion Singularity Master Fund slipped nearly 3%, avoiding larger declines by keeping its exposures low, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The two funds didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.

The technology selloff is being driven by expectations that Democrats, who have gained power in both houses of Congress, will push for stronger regulation of AI and slow the build out of data centres. In the US, Rob Pohly’s Samlyn Capital is dismissing senior analysts after cutting exposure to nearly every sector except global financials and Value Aligned Research Advisors, an AI-focused hedge fund, plunged 33% last month.

See also: Asian chip shares drop after US vote, bonds rise

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index tumbled as much as 5.3% on Friday, following a rout in the Nasdaq 100 on Thursday that wiped out a record US$2.3 trillion in market value. South Korea’s Kospi Index plunged as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker.

In Hong Kong, one broker said retail investors began flooding the firm with inquiries overnight, forcing staff to work overtime to calm nerves and discuss risk management strategies. He said the only advice for clients was to “run for the exit” as quickly as they can, and for margin traders to focus on lowering their leveraged bets.

Even so, the broker said the risk of widespread forced liquidations was somewhat reduced because his firm had begun urging clients weeks earlier to increase collateral on leveraged technology positions.

“We’re fielding queries about the AI selloff left and right,” said Hiroyuki Ueno, chief strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management in Tokyo. “Sell-side clients are struggling to explain what’s going on to their customers.”

While short-term investors can react quickly, larger institutional funds face more difficult choices, Ueno said.

For many investors across Asia, the key question is no longer whether AI valuations needed a reset, but how much further the selloff will go. Confidence has evaporated faster than liquidity, leaving traders searching for a floor in a market where few are willing to call a bottom.

“The impression I got from our team’s morning meeting is that the market is behaving irrationally,” said Hiroshi Namioka, chief strategist and fund manager at T&D Asset Management Co. “I wouldn’t go so far as to say it’s outright panic, but investors are finding it difficult to see upside.”

Market participants also pointed to options-related flows amplifying volatility as key technical levels gave way.

“It looks more like a position blowout than a fundamental rethinking of the future,” said Travis Lundy, a Hong Kong-based independent analyst who consults for hedge funds. “A bad October for some appears to have triggered early November unwinds which have cascaded.”

title: Japan’s GPIF fund keeps quarterly asset allocation little changed
article:
(Nov 6): Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) kept its allocations to domestic bonds and equities close to its 25% targets, signalling little change in its investment stance.

Speculation has been rife for months that the ¥314.4 trillion (US$2 trillion or $2.6 trillion) fund, one of the world’s largest public pension investors, may shift more money into its home market, potentially boosting Japanese stocks and bonds.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s suggestion in July that GPIF could buy more domestic assets fuelled the speculation, as did a surprise management meeting in August. The latest results, however, showed the fund sticking to the status quo, potentially damping expectations of an imminent shift.

GPIF allocated 26.49% of its portfolio to Japanese bonds and 24.80% to domestic stocks. Both remain within the tight ranges the fund has stuck to in recent years, even though it is allowed to deviate from those 25% targets by five to six percentage points.

While its allocation to Japanese bonds rose to 26.49% from 25.59% in June, the share tends to increase in March and September because of seasonal patterns in cash management of the country’s pension system.

See also: Japan’s Nikkei enters bear market as AI sell-off deepens

“It appears GPIF is barely making use of the permitted deviation ranges from its model portfolio. As of the end of September, it seems to be rebalancing its portfolio toward the 25% targets, as it has done in the past,” said Koji Okuda, an executive researcher at Daiichi Life Research Institute. “Judging from these results alone, there is no sign that GPIF is moving towards changing its model portfolio.”

Buying domestic assets could support Takaichi’s agenda by helping curb yen weakness and lower Japanese government bond yields as she seeks to boost fiscal spending to stimulate growth.

For GPIF, however, the bar for changing its allocations is high. The fund has stressed that its sole goal is to secure pension benefits for future generations.

See also: Toyota soars most since 1987 on higher profit outlook, buybacks

Market participants have said the GPIF is unlikely to shift its holdings without a clear investment rationale, though they have not ruled out changes given the influence of Japan’s Health Ministry, which oversees the fund, in setting its target returns.

In the three months through September, the fund suffered its first quarterly loss in six quarters, declining 1.7% as global bond prices fell and the yen strengthened. Still, it outperformed its benchmarks by five basis points in domestic bonds and 13 basis points in foreign bonds, while Japanese stocks underperformed by eight basis points. Foreign stocks performed in line with their benchmark.

title: 新加坡三大银行业绩好坏参半 分析师对进场看法不一
NEX商场一半股权寻买主 要价12亿元至12.5亿元
区域AI抛售潮与银行股继续受压 海指周五败跌2.21%
评股论经：中国银河国际下调百汇生命信托目标价 继续建议增持
